summary: This document updates RFC 8253, which describes using TLS to secure PCEP (PCEPS). It adds restrictions on what PCEPS implementations do when they support more than one TLS version.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds two TLS connection rules for PCEPS, which uses TLS to protect PCEP. Implementations must prefer their latest supported TLS version and must not use early data with TLS 1.3 or later.

questions: does pceps allow tls 1.3 early data
which tls version should pceps prefer
does pceps allow tls early data
subtitle: PCEPS implementations must prefer the latest TLS version and avoid early data.

tldr.problem: RFC 8253 did not specify how PCEPS implementations should choose among supported TLS versions or use TLS 1.3 early data.
tldr.mechanism: Implementations supporting several TLS versions must prefer the latest; PCEPS implementations supporting TLS 1.3 or later must not use early data.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 8253 and leaves its other connection rules unchanged.

facts.label: Version preference
facts.value: Prefer the latest supported TLS version

facts.label: Early data
facts.value: MUST NOT be used with TLS 1.3 or later

today: RFC 9916 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. It updates RFC 8253; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 9916.

sections.title: Scope of the Update
sections.content:
RFC 8253 specifies TLS connection restrictions for PCEPS, the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) to protect the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). This document adds requirements for implementations that support more than one TLS version and restricts TLS 1.3 early data.

All other RFC 8253 provisions remain unchanged, including connection initiation, message framing, connection closure, certificate validation, peer identity and failure handling.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEPS uses TLS to protect PCEP messages. This update adds rules for TLS version choice and early data, while leaving other connection behavior unchanged.

sections.title: Prefer the Latest TLS Version
sections.content: An implementation that supports multiple TLS versions MUST prefer to negotiate the latest TLS version. The RFC gives TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 as an example and points to Section 4.2.1 of RFC 9846 for version negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: If an implementation supports more than one TLS version, it must prefer the latest version when negotiating with its peer.

sections.title: Do Not Use Early Data
sections.content:
PCEPS implementations that support TLS 1.3 or later MUST NOT use early data, also called 0-RTT data. In TLS 1.3, early data lets a client send data in its first flight of messages to a server, using a Pre-Shared Key shared with that server.

The RFC explains that early data has weaker security properties than later TLS-protected data: it is not forward secret and has no protection against replay between connections. TLS 1.3 can be used without early data.
sections.plainLanguage: Early data is sent before the full TLS exchange finishes. PCEPS must not use it because it has weaker security and can be replayed between connections.
